Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette:
Adjoa was seventy-one when it happened, though she often feels like she has been seventy-seven her entire life since. She had been a politician for decades, a woman known for her steady voice and her refusal to be intimidated, first in her home country and then in the United States after she and her husband emigrated. The man who beat her was not a stranger; he was her lover, a man she had trusted with the keys to her apartment and the passwords to her phone. The night it ended, he had grown quiet during dinner, and she had mistaken his silence for tenderness. When she reached for his hand, he struck her across the face with such force that she tasted blood before she felt the pain. She remembers the wet sound, the sting, the way her glasses flew across the room, but the minutes after that are a blur of broken images-a shoe on the carpet, the glint of a lamp, her own voice saying something she cannot recall. She has never been able to piece together how she got from the dining table to the bathroom floor, and that missing gap haunts her more than the blows themselves. Every time she tries to complete the memory, a wall slams down inside her, and she pushes it away before she can see what comes next.

In the months that followed, Adjoa found herself scanning rooms before she entered them, her eyes darting to corners and doorways. She began to notice the way certain people raised their voices in meetings, even calmly, and her chest would tighten before she could stop it. A colleague's raised eyebrow during a committee vote sent a spike of alarm through her that made no sense in the moment but felt utterly real. She came to believe that she had been permanently damaged by that night, that something essential in her had broken and could not be repaired. She told herself she would never feel normal emotions again, that the part of her that had once laughed easily and trusted freely was gone for good. This conviction made her hypervigilant: if she could not trust her own feelings, she had to rely on constant scanning for danger, and so she began checking behind her as she walked to her car, especially at dusk, when the shadows lengthened and the world felt less safe. She found herself startling at the sound of a door closing too sharply, her heart hammering for minutes afterward, and each time she felt that surge of fear, the memory of that night pushed closer to the surface, demanding to be finished.

The weight of her mistrust grew heavy. She had believed, before the assault, that people were fundamentally decent; now she was certain they could not be trusted, and this belief colored every interaction. When a young aide approached her with a concern, Adjoa found herself bracing for an attack, reading threat into the aide's earnest tone. These moments of perceived danger triggered the memory of her partner's quiet anger before the first blow, and the guilt would rise-a hot, shameful wave-because she had not seen it coming, because she had loved him, because she had stayed. She began to avoid physical proximity whenever possible, stepping back from handshakes and standing at the far end of conference tables. In her office, she kept her desk angled so that no one could approach from behind, and she flinched when a staff member touched her shoulder to get her attention. The sight of blood, even a paper cut, sent her reeling into a state of high alert, her mind racing with fragments of that incomplete memory.

Her husband, a gentle man who had never raised a hand to her, noticed the changes. She stopped wanting to walk with him in the evening, claiming fatigue. She stopped wanting to be touched at all. He asked what was wrong, and she could not tell him-not because she did not trust him, but because she was afraid that speaking the words aloud would make the damage permanent in a way she could not undo. So she withdrew further, and the loneliness of that withdrawal confirmed what she already believed: that she was changed for the worse, that she would never feel normal again. At night, alone in the dark, she lay rigid, listening to every creak of the house, certain that someone was coming. She felt the guilt press down on her chest, and she pushed the memory away again, incomplete, unfinished, always waiting.

What finally brought Adjoa to seek help was a moment in a public hearing when a witness raised his voice in frustration-not at her, not even loudly-and she felt her vision narrow and her breath stop. She excused herself, walked to the restroom, and stood gripping the sink, staring at her own reflection. She was afraid that she was losing the ability to do her job, the one thing she had always been sure of. She was afraid that the missing pieces of that night would never come back, and that she would spend the rest of her life jumping at shadows, waiting for a blow that had already landed.
